messages.author: 8f3a6b28f0ffde17
messages.subject: Session-level covariates
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to model density from capture-recapture data as a function of an RSF (obtained from telemetry data), and a number of session-level covariates. Each session is a different year (9 years). Session-level covariates include the following:

-Whether there was construction that year or not

-summer precipitation

-summer temperature

-winter precipitation

-winter temperature

 

Two of my models look like this:

1)     D ~ RSF + Construction + precip.summer + temp.summer, lambda0 ~ g, sigma ~ g

2)     D ~ RSF + Construction + precip.winter + temp.summer, lambda0 ~ g, sigma ~ g

g represents three variables that affect detection probability.

 

As exploratory analyses, I ran null models on each year separately. If I run the following linear regressions using the density estimates from those null models, Model b gives a much better R-squared than Model a (b=0.5, a=0.3).

a)      Density ~ Construction + precip.summer + temp.summer

b)     Density ~ Construction + precip.winter + temp.summer

However, if I run these combinations in a multi-session SECR model as in Models 1 and 2 above, Model 1 is better than Model 2.

 

I was expecting Model 2 to be better than Model 1. Maybe I am not understanding something. Could someone please enlighten me as to why this might not be the case? I would really like to know what I am missing here.

Based on my first two SECR models above, am I using the right approach to model variation in annual Density?

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you

Joel

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Session-level covariates
parts:
Hi Joel
Some random thoughts
1. R^2 = 0.5 is not that much 'better' than R^ = 0.3
2. I assume you are relying on AIC: just how big was the difference?
3. 'secr' (if that is what your are using) defaults to a log link for density, which is probably not what you used in the ad hoc annual regressions and may behave differently
4. An identity link may be better, but it can throw up its own problems in maximisation (can be fixed by setting the 'typsize' argument of nlm to bring all parameters onto comparable scales - only go there if you need to!)
5. I hope you have lots of data to support this model!
Murray
